New shared syntax cannot use these\nadapter differences as an implicit parity exception.\nPython, PHP, and Go express link groups through nested links and collections;\nthey do not expose JS's `LinksGroup` class. Java lacks the full\n`FormatConfig` object, while default formatting is covered by the shared corpus.\nRust's compile-time macro and tuple adapters are host-specific exceptions in the\nother seven bindings. These existing differences must not be silently represented\nas implemented APIs.\n## Generated code\nAll eight language libraries are hand-written. JavaScript's Peggy parser and\nC#'s Pegasus parser are generated from hand-written grammars within their own\nlanguage. There is currently no JS-to-Rust translation pipeline. Meta-language's\nstructural translation can be explored in `experiments/`, but a translated\nmodule must prove semantic equivalence and have a regenerate-and-diff check\nbefore it replaces the working library. See `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the\ndevelopment order.\n# Lossless reference literals, version 1\nStarting with Links Notation 0.24.0, every binding (C++ from its first release)\nsupports an explicit UTF-8 literal for any reference identifier or value:\n```ebnf\nreference_literal = \"~1{\", { hex_digit, hex_digit }, \"}\" ;\nhex_digit         = \"0\"..\"9\" | \"a\"..\"f\" | \"A\"..\"F\" ;\n```\nThe body is the hexadecimal encoding of the reference's UTF-8 bytes. Encoders\nwrite lowercase hex; decoders accept either case. There is no whitespace\ninside the literal. `~1{}` is the empty string, `~1{00}` is U+0000,\n`~1{0d0a}` is CR followed by LF, and `~1{f09f9880}` is U+1F600.\nThe literal represents one reference, so it can appear before a link's colon,\ninside a group, or in an indented link:\n```text\n(~1{}: ~1{00} ~1{0d0a} ~1{f09f9880})\n```\nUTF-8 must be well formed: incomplete sequences, overlong encodings, surrogate\ncode points, and values above U+10FFFF are errors. An odd hex length, a missing\nclosing brace, non-hex content, or any version other than exactly `1` is also\nan error. Parsers refuse reserved malformed literals rather than returning\ntheir spelling as a reference. Decoding preserves every scalar, including a\nleading U+FEFF, combining marks, controls, line endings and whitespace. It\nperforms no trimming, newline conversion, or Unicode normalization.\n## Formatting and compatibility\nNative formatting and binary-to-text formatting share the same reference\nencoder. They use literals for empty strings, C0 controls (U+0000–U+001F),\nand DEL (U+007F). Other references retain readable bare or quoted spelling.\nFor quoting, the encoder chooses `'`, `\"`, or a backtick different from the\nfirst character, and uses an odd delimiter width greater than every run of\nthat delimiter in the body. The existing n-quote grammar then returns the\nbody exactly, even when it contains all three delimiters. Backslashes are\nordinary characters; they do not introduce escapes.\nThis is an explicitly versioned grammar extension. At a reference boundary,\nthe prefix `~` followed by one or more ASCII digits and `{` is reserved.\nAn existing reference such as `~1{61}` must now be written as `'~1{61}'` to\nretain that spelling; unquoted `~1{61}` means `a`. Formatters automatically\nquote these names. Existing quoted references, including legacy empty quote\npairs, still parse. The old ambiguous empty identifier spelling can span\nanother quote pair, so new formatters always write `~1{}` instead.\nUpgrade readers to 0.24.0 before sending literals. Older parsers treat this\nCHANGELOG.md:458:- Seven-language binary interoperability CI, native-model round trips, packet streams,\ndocs/protocol/binary-links-notation.md:242:parser metadata are not stored. [2026-11-01T11:25:08.651Z] [INFO]         "content": "# History of attempts toward true links visuals\n\nThis history answers [issue #31][issue-31]: how did attempts to visualize links that can refer to other links develop, and what did each attempt achieve? It follows the references in the issue, their original discussions and code, relevant public work in [LinksPlatform][linksplatform] and [Deep Foundation][deep-foundation], and the experiments preserved here. Sources were checked on **2026-10-11**\n\nThis is an inventory of identified public attempts, open to additions as earlier material is recovered. Dates identify a public comment, commit, or archived artifact, as specified below; they do not automatically establish a project's invention or release date. A source or demo link records evidence, not a guarantee that an old demo still runs in a current browser.\n\n## What the visual needs to express\n\nIn the [links theory][theory-doublets], a doublet-link has a reference of its own and two references to links, conventionally source and target. For example:\n\n```text\n1: (1, 1)   a link whose source and target both refer to itself\n2: (2, 2)   another such link\n3: (1, 2)   a link between those two links\n4: (3, 2)   a link starting from link 3 and ending at link 2\n5: (3, 4)   a link between two links that themselves connect links\n```\n\nThe theory's [network illustrations][theory-figures] depict self-reference using a closed arrow resembling an infinity symbol. The practical visual goal is to make a link's identity and its source/target references readable, including when a reference names another connecting link. Recursive structure and self-reference also need to remain understandable during interaction.\n\nSeveral approaches below use ordinary graph nodes as proxies for links. Those encodings can preserve the references and support useful tools. Whether the picture shows a connection to the actual curve, to a proxy node, or only to a nested textual representation is a separate question. The descriptions distinguish these choices rather than treating every graph view as the same result.\n\n## Timeline\n\n| Date or period | Attempt and evidence | Contribution and remaining boundary |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| 2015-09-16 archive; one page stamped 2011-05-11 | LinksPlatform [Web UI prototypes 1 and 2][web-ui-original] | Hyperlinked descriptions and nested trees expose link structure. The HTML mirror timestamp is evidence of an older artifact, not a verified launch date. |\n| 2015-11-12 | LinksPlatform [doublet][doublet-symbol] and [triplet][triplet-symbol] SVG symbols | Nested circles explore how one link can contain references; these are symbols rather than an editor for a network. |\n| 2016-01-10–14 | Konard's [Cytoscape.js request #1217][cytoscape-request] and the [maintainer's decision][cytoscape-decision] | An edge whose endpoints name edges did not display. Native support was declined because it conflicted with Cytoscape's graph model and algorithms; intermediary and compound nodes were suggested. |\n| 2016-01-12 | LinksPlatform [closed-link Bézier experiment][closed-link-commit] | An animated, draggable curve explores a link starting and ending at itself. These dates mark source milestones, not the first Deep.Case release. |\n| 2025-02–04 | This repository's [straight link][straight-link-commit], [H-fractal][h-fractal-commit], [blueprint][blueprint-commit], and [IK experiments][ik-commit] | Geometry develops from a directed line to recursive layouts, editable splines, and constrained link animation. |\n| 2025-04-17 onward | Deep Foundation [DeepVisual implementation][deepvisual-commit] | Python plots include infinity-shaped loops and arrows between previously positioned links. The implementation has ordering and representation limits. |\n| 2026-03 | This repository's [grid PRs][grid-pr] | Several links can be displayed together, with interactive endpoints and grid snapping. |\n| 2026-05-08 | LinksPlatform [doublets-web playground][doublets-web-commit] | Live doublets data gets an SVG graph view beside a JavaScript editor; attachment is to ID nodes rather than to a represented link's curve. |\n| 2026-06 | This repository's [proportion fix][grid-fix-pr] and [drawing-to-link demo][draw-pr] | Multiple-link geometry becomes consistent; drawn endpoints can pin to another link's center and follow its movement. |\n| 2026-08-22 | [Issue #31][issue-31] | The request to bring these attempts together into a traceable history. |\n\nThe rest of this document explains the implementation choices behind these milestones. Chronology alone does not imply that one project reused another's code.\n\n## LinksPlatform: symbols, self-reference, and recursive browsing\n\n### Early web interfaces and symbols\n\nThe [2015 archive commit][web-ui-original] contains two earlier interfaces. [Prototype 1][web-ui-1] presents source/linker/target descriptions as hyperlinks and lists referring links. Its HTML says it was mirrored on 2011-05-11. [Prototype 2][web-ui-2] represents descriptions using nested lists. The public commit establishes their preservation by September 2015; the mirror header alone cannot date\n\nThe November 2015 [doublet][doublet-symbol] and [triplet][triplet-symbol] pages represent a containing circle with two or three smaller circles. The [2020 circles-ring page][circles-ring-source] generalizes that construction interactively. They explore visual vocabulary for reference structure, without demonstrating a connection from one drawn arrow to another.\n\nThe January 2016 [closed-link experiment][closed-link-source] uses seven initial control points with the first, middle, and last at the same location. D3 animates Bézier interpolation and lets the user drag the controls. Its [introduction commit][closed-link-commit] explicitly identifies self-reference as the purpose. This makes the geometry of a self-referencing link visible, but has no collecti\n\n### The Cytoscape request and the two workarounds\n\nOn 2016-01-10, [Konard asked Cytoscape.js][cytoscape-request] to display an edge whose source and target were the IDs of two other edges. The request also included sketches of node-to-edge, edge-to-edge, and recursively encapsulated structures. Konard [clarified][cytoscape-clarification] that the intended relation was binary, with links as both endpoints, rather than an arbitrary-arity hyperedge.\n\nOn January 13, [Max Franz declined native support][cytoscape-decision] after discussing it with the team: Cytoscape's traversal and other algorithms depended on its node/edge model. He suggested application-level nodes or an extension; [the next reply][cytoscape-alternatives] explained intermediary and compound nodes. This records a library design decision, rather than establishing a prohibition o\n\nKonard [posted two implemented examples on January 15][cytoscape-demos-comment], also preserved in the [introduction commit][cytoscape-demos-commit]:\n\n| Example | Mechanism in the source | What it demonstrates |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| [Intermediary nodes][intermediary-source] · [demo][intermediary-demo] | Holding a node adds source and target nodes with edges `source → node → target`; holding again removes its generated descendants. | A link can be represented by a node and two reference edges, with repeated expansion. The link is visually split into graph elements. |\n| [Compound nodes][compound-source] · [demo][compound-demo] | Holding a node creates two child nodes and an edge inside that parent; holding again removes the children. | Recursive containment can be explored, while connections still have graph nodes as endpoints. |\n\nBoth handlers rerun the Dagre layout. They establish working responses to the suggestion, with different visual tradeoffs from attaching a connector to an intact link curve.\n\n### Later viewers and explanatory material\n\nThe [RawDoubletsViewer alpha commit][raw-viewer-commit] dates to July 19, 2020. Its [Win32 list-view code][raw-viewer-source] displays stored records, including source and target fields. It supplies direct inspection of doublets, rather than a geometric renderer of connections between them.\n\n[InfiniteDepthTreeWebUIPrototype][tree-prototype] was [moved out of Documentation on July 20, 2020][tree-extraction]. Its README describes viewing and editing deep graphs through a tree, including structures with self-references. [react-deep-tree][react-tree] explicitly identifies that prototype as its starting point and provides a React component for navigating nested content. The tree representa\n\nThe [September 2021 stack drawings][stack-commit] preserve SVG, raster, and editable artwork under [Documentation's visualization archive][visualizations-archive]. The [November introduction animation draft][intro-animation-commit] adds an SVG animation and an HTML wrapper. These are explanatory visual artifacts; neither commit establishes a general interactive links editor.\n\n## GoJS: an early implementation using link label nodes\n\nOn [March 25, 2016][gojs-comment], Konard linked to the GoJS example in the Cytoscape discussion. [Issue #31][issue-31] recalls it as the only implementation he had seen before the later supporters. The comment establishes that the example was known by that date; it does not establish when Northwoods first released it.\n\nThe [official sample][gojs-sample] shows node-to-link and link-to-link connections. It explains that link-owned label nodes serve as connection points and that newly drawn links receive label nodes automatically. Moving the original nodes updates the connections. This achieves the visual effect through GoJS's node/label mechanism, while retaining separate node and link types in the underlying diag\n\n## Community support: cytoscape-edge-connections\n\nIn [November 2018][cytoscape-support], another user raised layout concerns with intermediary nodes. In [December][associative-support], Jörg Richter distinguished the associative model from the graph model. On [January 2, 2019][extension-announcement], he announced an extension, originally linked under `jri/cytoscape-edge-connections` and now hosted at [dmx-systems/cytoscape-edge-connections][ext\n\nIts [version history][extension-history] dates the functional initial version to December 30, 2018, and the general-purpose version to January 2, 2019. The [implementation documentation][extension-mechanism] describes an auxiliary node superimposed on each connectable edge, synchronized with its position. It keeps the original edge intact, unlike the two-edge intermediary representation. The [demo\n\nThe API accepts edge IDs as endpoints through the extension's `addEdge`/`addEdges` methods. Ordinary Cytoscape edge creation does not provide that behavior. Auxiliary nodes remain the actual attachment points in the renderer; this is an extension-based encoding rather than native unification of nodes and edges. It is a concrete community response to the earlier limitation.\n\n## Deep Foundation: graph projections and direct plots\n\n### Deep.Case in 2D and 3D\n\nThe available [deepcase-app source history][deepcase-app-commit] includes Cytoscape components by July 2022. In July 2023, [deepcase][deepcase-package-commit] contains the extracted visualization package; [deepcase-app's README][deepcase-app] identifies the app as using that package. These are verifiable repository milestones, not a claim about the first version of Deep.Case.\n\nIn the default [Cytoscape element builder][deepcase-elements], each stored link gets a `link-node` carrying its ID. Separate `link-from`, `link-to`, and optional `link-type` edges connect that node to nodes representing the referenced links. Because references point to link IDs, another link can refer to a connecting link through its node representation. Custom Cyto handlers are also present; this\n\nThe [A-Frame graph-data builder][aframe-data] also creates a node for each link and reference edges, including `from → link → to` and type references. Its [addition in July 2023][aframe-commit] records a 3D visualization path. Both projections preserve addressable links through graph nodes; they do not demonstrate endpoints attached directly to arbitrary displayed curves.\n\n### DeepVisual\n\nThe [DeepVisual repository][deepvisual] describes a Python visualization library. Its code was [introduced on April 17, 2025][deepvisual-commit]. In the reviewed [implementation][deepvisual-source], `visualize_link_doublet` draws infinity-shaped loops, stores positions for ordinary links, and draws further arrows to the midpoints of those links. This is a direct attempt to show links between links\n\nThe code also defines its boundaries: link IDs are derived from `DataFrame` row indices plus one; positions are collected during row-order traversal; and the displayed endpoints must already have usable positions. The deeper arrows' positions are not registered in the same map for further attachment. Also, its loop classification tests `from == to`, which alone does not establish that both referen\n\n## This repository: geometry, layout, and connected drawing\n\nThe [February 2025 starting point][straight-link-commit] builds a directed line with start/end markers and draggable endpoints. The [H-fractal attempt][h-fractal-commit] in March explores recursive spatial structure using smaller arrows. April brings the [spline blueprint][blueprint-commit], [distance constraints][distance-commit], [half-link animation][half-link-commit], and [FABRIK-driven bluepr\n\nThe current pages preserve several approaches:\n\n| Page | Purpose | Boundary relevant to this history |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| [index.html](../index.html) | Directed line, markers, and draggable endpoints. | One line's appearance and controls. |\n| [H-fractal.html](../H-fractal.html) | Click-driven recursive subdivision with straight arrows. | A generated fractal layout rather than an editor for arbitrary stored references. |\n| [blueprint.html](../blueprint.html) | Configurable link spline with control points and markers. | A single link's geometry. |\n| [distance-constrained-blueprint.html](../distance-constrained-blueprint.html) | Endpoint dragging with constrained half-chains. | An alternative single-link constraint experiment. |\n| [fabrik.html](../fabrik.html) and [fabrik-horizontal.html](../fabrik-horizontal.html) | Vertical/horizontal constant-curvature IK experiments. | Half-chain behavior, not a network. |\n| [animated-blueprint.html](../animated-blueprint.html) | IK-driven link geometry with shared rendering modules. | How one link bends and loops. |\n| [tests.html](../tests.html) | Geometry cases including loops and wave-like configurations. | A geometry test harness. |\n| [grid.html](../grid.html) | Several colored links with fixed centers and movable endpoints. | Spatial placement and snapping; coincident positions alone do not create persistent link-ID references. |\n| [draw.html](../draw.html) | Freehand strokes become links; endpoints can pin to existing centers. | Explicit center attachment, with geometry derived from drawing. |\n\nThe March 2026 [grid additions][grid-pr] were followed by [interaction changes][grid-controls-pr] and [control-style corrections][grid-style-pr]. The [June proportion fix][grid-fix-pr] reconciled their appearance with the single-link blueprint. This sequence matters because showing several shapes consistently is another step beyond producing one attractive link.\n\nThe [June drawing demo PR][draw-pr] adds a more explicit connection mechanism. In [draw-link.mjs](../js/draw-link.mjs), `startAnchorId` and `endAnchorId` refer to other drawn links, and `applyCenterAnchors` resolves their centers. The existing [drawing E2E tests](../tests/draw.e2e.test.mjs) verify that a child endpoint stays pinned when its parent center moves. This demonstrates references to othe\n\n### Preserved attempts\n\nThe directory name `failed-attempts` records the repository's own classification. [Issue 27's case study](case-studies/issue-27/README.md) and [issue 28's case study](case-studies/issue-28/README.md) explain the drawing and grid work in detail.\n\n## LinksPlatform doublets-web: live data with a graph view\n\nThe [May 8, 2026 playground commit][doublets-web-commit] adds an editor and graph view to [doublets-web][doublets-web]. This dates the visualization addition, separately from the older storage-binding project. In its [SVG renderer][doublets-web-renderer], link IDs and endpoint IDs receive circular graph-node positions, while each record becomes a line or loop labeled by its ID.\n\nThis gives a useful visual companion to live doublets queries. A reference to another link reaches that link's ID node, whose position is distinct from its labeled line. It therefore belongs in the history as a storage-connected graph projection with a different representation from curve-to-curve attachment.\n\n## What these attempts leave to explore\n\nThe sources show progress in several directions: readable reference structure, closed self-referencing shapes, attachments that follow a moving curve, browsing deep data, consistent geometry for multiple links, and explicit references between drawn links.\n\nThe remaining goal is to combine those properties: stable identity, arbitrary source/target references, self-reference and cycles, understandable recursive structure, and layout that stays readable as links move. Single-link geometry demos, tree browsers, and graph encodings provide evidence for parts of that goal. Their existence alone does not establish a complete solution.\n\nTo extend this record, add a primary source and its date, describe the actual representation, and state what was demonstrated versus what remains unverified. Preserve original project names and moved-repository links. Where an older artifact's date or behavior is uncertain, record the uncertainty instead of assigning an invented milestone.\n\n[issue-31]: Add a demo named `draw.html`.\n   - Implemented as a standalone HTML demo following the existing `blueprint.html` and `grid.html` pattern.\n\n2. Support Apple Pencil, iPad Pro, and similar pen/touch hardware.\n   - Implemented with Pointer Events on the SVG drawing surface and `touch-action:none`.\n\n3. Drawing a line creates a link where the first point is start, the last point is end, and the middle of the drawn path is center.\n   - Implemented in `js/draw-link.mjs`; center is computed at 50% of polyline path length, not by raw point index.\n\n4. Keep the path close to the original drawing.\n   - The drawn polyline is simplified by distance, capped for performance, and rendered through the existing blueprint Catmull-Rom-to-cubic path helper.\n\n5. Preserve start, end, center, and freely placed intermediate points.\n   - Rendered controls use green start, red end, black center, and blue intermediate circles.\n\n6. Match `blueprint.html` element style exactly.\n   - The demo reuses `buildBlueprintPathData`, `appendBlueprintEndpointMarkers`, `createBlueprintMetrics`, and `CONTROL_POINT_COLORS`.\n   - Control circles keep transparent fill, dashed `4 2` outlines, fixed 1px stroke, and radius derived from the same grid spacing.\n\n7. Support drawing links from centers of other links.\n   - If a new stroke starts or ends within the center snap radius of an existing link, that endpoint is anchored to the source center.\n\n8. Keep pinned endpoints attached when the source center moves.\n   - Anchored endpoints are resolved at render time via `applyCenterAnchors`.\n\n9. Support as many drawn links as practical.\n   - Links are stored as independent polyline data, rendered in one SVG layer, and persisted in localStorage. Each stroke is simplified and capped to avoid unbounded point growth.\n\n10. Provide two input modes: select/move and draw.\n    - `Draw` mode creates links and does not move existing controls.\n    - `Select` mode moves free controls and parent centers. Pinned endpoints are non-interactive so the source center remains selectable.\n\n11. The badges read live from the package\n> registries, so they always reflect the latest published state.\nUniversal serialization library to encode/decode objects to/from Links Notation format. Available in **Python**, **JavaScript**, **Rust**, and **C#** with identical functionality and API design.\n## 🌍 Multi-Language Support\nThis library provides universal serialization and deserialization with built-in support for circular references and complex object graphs in:\n- **[Python](python/)** - Full implementation for Python 3.13+\n- **[JavaScript](js/)** - Full implementation for Node.js 22.11+\n- **[Rust](rust/)** - Full implementation for Rust 1.87+ (tests require 1.88+)\n- **[C#](csharp/)** - Full implementation for .NET 10.0+\nAll implementations share the same design philosophy and provide feature parity.\n## Features\n- **Universal Serialization**: Encode objects to Links Notation format\n- **Type Support**: Handle all common types in each language:\n  - **Python**: `None`, `bool`, `int`, `float`, `str`, `list`, `dict`\n  - **JavaScript**: `null`, `undefined`, `boolean`, `number`, `string`, `Array`, `Object`\n  - **Rust**: `LinoValue` enum with `Null`, `Bool`, `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Array`, `Object`\n  - **C#**: `null`, `bool`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `string`, `List<object?>`, `Dictionary<string, object?>`\n  - Special float/number values: `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`\n- **Readable by Default**: In every language `encode()` writes indented, plain-text Links Notation; the previous single-line base64 form stays available as `encode_compact()` (alias `encode_obfuscated()`)\n- **One Record per Line**: `encode_line()` writes the same readable document on one line and `decode_line()` reads it back exactly, so an append-only log stays greppable, tailable and countable by `wc -l`\n- **Object Identity**: Shared references and circular references are preserved by the compact format via object ids; the readable format is a plain tree and raises a circular-reference error instead\n- **Full Unicode**: Strings are always written as text — a newline stays a newline, a tab stays a tab, and every word stays greppable; only the characters a form cannot carry are percent-escaped, in a value marked individually as `(escaped \"…\")`\n- **Opt-in Tracing**: Set `LINO_CODEC_DEBUG=1` to trace encoding and decoding, the same way in every language\n- **Simple API**: Easy-to-use `encode()` and `decode()` functions\n- **JSON/Lino Conversion**: Convert between JSON and Links Notation (JavaScript)\n- **Reference Escaping**: Properly escape strings for Links Notation format (JavaScript)\n- **Fuzzy Matching**: String similarity utilities for finding matches (JavaScript)\n- **Indented Format**: Human-readable indented Links Notation format for display and debugging\n## Quick Start\n### Python\n```bash\npip install lino-objects-codec\n```\n```python\nfrom link_notation_objects_codec import encode, decode\n# Encode and decode\ndata = {\"name\": \"Alice\", \"age\": 30, \"active\": True}\nencoded = encode(data)\ndecoded = decode(encoded)\nassert decoded == data\n```\n### JavaScript\n```bash\nnpm install lino-objects-codec\n```\n```javascript\nimport { encode, decode } from \"lino-objects-codec\";\n// `encode` produces readable, indented Links Notation by default\nconst data = { name: \"Alice\", age: 30, active: true };\nconst encoded = encode({ obj: data });\nconst decoded = decode({ notation: encoded });\nconsole.log(JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(data)); // true\n```\n### Rust\n```toml\n[dependencies]\nlino-objects-codec = \"0.1\"\n```\n```rust\nuse lino_objects_codec::{encode, decode, LinoValue};\n// Encode and decode\nlet data = LinoValue::object([\n    (\"name\", LinoValue::String(\"Alice\".to_string())),\n    (\"age\", LinoValue::Int(30)),\n    (\"active\", LinoValue::Bool(true)),\n]);\n// `encode` produces readable, indented Links Notation\nlet encoded = encode(&data);\nassert_eq!(encoded, \"(\\n  name \\\"Alice\\\"\\n  age 30\\n  active true\\n)\");\nlet decoded = decode(&encoded).unwrap();\nassert_eq!(decoded, data);\n```\n```lino\n(\n  name \"Alice\"\n  age 30\n  active true\n)\n```\nFor an append-only log, `encode_line()` writes the same document on one line:\n```lino\n(o: (name \"Alice\") (age 30) (active true))\n```\n```python\nfrom link_notation_objects_codec import encode_line, decode_line\ndecode_line(encode_line(data)) == data\n```\n```javascript\nimport { encodeLine, decodeLine } from \"lino-objects-codec\";\ndecodeLine({ notation: encodeLine({ obj: data }) });\n```\n```rust\nuse lino_objects_codec::{decode_line, encode_line};\nassert_eq!(decode_line(&encode_line(&data)).unwrap(), data);\n```\n```csharp\nvar line = Codec.EncodeLine(data);\nvar record = Codec.DecodeLine(line);\n```\nThe single-line base64 form is still available as `encode_compact()` (alias\n`encode_obfuscated()`) in every language, and `decode()` accepts all three forms.\n### C#\n```bash\ndotnet add package Lino.Objects.Codec\n```\n```csharp\nusing Lino.Objects.Codec;\n// Encode and decode\nvar data = new Dictionary<string, object?>\n{\n    { \"name\", \"Alice\" },\n    { \"age\", 30 },\n    { \"active\", true }\n};\nvar encoded = Codec.Encode(data);\nvar decoded = Codec.Decode(encoded) as Dictionary<string, object?>;\nConsole.WriteLine(decoded?[\"name\"]); // Alice\n```\n## Repository Structure\n```\n.\n├── python/           # Python implementation\n│   ├── src/         # Source code\n│   ├── tests/       # Test suite\n│   ├── examples/    # Usage examples\n│   └── README.md    # Python-specific docs\n├── js/              # JavaScript implementation\n│   ├── src/         # Source code\n│   ├── tests/       # Test suite\n│   ├── examples/    # Usage examples\n│   └── README.md    # JavaScript-specific docs\n├── rust/            # Rust implementation\n│   ├── src/         # Source code\n│   ├── examples/    # Usage examples\n│   └── README.md    # Rust-specific docs\n├── csharp/          # C# implementation\n│   ├── src/         # Source code\n│   ├── tests/       # Test suite",

There is nothing\n   stopping a user (or randomizer) from rotating an elbow backwards or\n   stretching a knee inward. Numbers are also displayed in raw radians, which\n   are unintuitive.\n3. **Animations don't blend smoothly.** When idle gaze tracking is on and the\n   user clicks the `nod` or `shake` gesture, the head jumps because:\n   - Programmatic gestures **replace** look-at head contributions for their\n     entire duration (head bone is locked to gesture rotation while\n     `gestureActive`, then suddenly handed back to the smoother).\n   - The look-at smoother is reset across the discontinuity.\n     The result is a visible snap at gesture start and gesture end.\n4. **There is no on-model rotation gizmo.** All rotation control lives in the\n   side drawer; users have asked for the editor-style ring gizmos shown in\n   most 3D editors (Blender / Unity / VRoid), one ring per axis around the\n   currently-selected joint, with hover/tap to switch joints. Both desktop\n   and mobile control flows should work.\n\nThis case study compiles the requirements, the anatomical reference data, the\nrelevant three.js / VRM library affordances, the proposed solution, and the\nremaining open questions.\n\n## Requirements (from the issue)\n\n| #   | Requirement                                                                                                                                                                                 |\n| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| R1  | Improve the `wave` gesture so the hand oscillates at the wrist, with a raised forearm, matching the reference image.                                                                        |\n| R2  | Default to **anatomically possible** rotations only — every joint slider must clamp to its biological range (per axis).                                                                     |\n| R3  | Display rotations as **degrees** in `−360..0..360` range (clamped to anatomical limits where relevant).                                                                                     |\n| R4  | Add an optional in-viewport joint gizmo (rings around each axis, similar to Blender / Unity). One joint visible at a time; hover (desktop) / tap (mobile) to switch joints. Off by default. |\n| R5  | Confirm full mobile + desktop support (touch & pointer interaction). Experimental — off by default.                                                                                         |\n| R6  | All animations should additively combine (relative deltas, summed each frame); transitions between gestures / look-at / idle must be smooth (no snaps).                                     |\n| R7  | Specifically: `yes` (nod) and `no` (shake) gestures should overlay on top of camera tracking instead of replacing it, and start/end without jumps.                                          |\n| R8  | Compile this case study at `docs/case-studies/issue-28/` with timeline, requirements, root causes, libraries researched, and proposed solutions.                                            |\n\n## Reference image\n\n![Wave reference](./reference-wave.png)\n\nThe reference shows the right arm raised so the hand is **above the head**\n(upper arm rotated up ~−90° around the local Z axis from VRM rest), the\nforearm bent ~90° forward (negative X on `rightLowerArm`), and the hand\nkept roughly vertical with the palm forward — a classic open-hand greeting.\n==== #18\nhttps://vrm.dev/en/showcase\n\nhttps://github.com/m3-org/CharacterStudio\n\nhttps://studio.m3org.com\n\nhttps://hub.vroid.com/en\n\nFree models:\n\nhttps://hub.vroid.com/en/characters/2843975675147313744/models/5644550979324015604\nhttps://hub.vroid.com/en/characters/7939147878897061040/models/2292219474373673889\nhttps://hub.vroid.com/en/characters/1248981995540129234/models/8640547963669442173\n==== #23\nhttps://github.com/Mirza-Samad-Ahmed-Baig/airi\n\nhttps://airi.moeru.ai/settings/models (Live2D, VRM)\n==== #24\nIt can be helpful to find all related projects\n==== #38",

blank lines and indentation are preserved.\nconst record = { id: \"doc\", obj: { t: \"line1\\n\\n  line2\" } };\nparseIndented({ text: formatIndented(record) }); // returns record\n```\n**Python:**\n```python\nfrom link_notation_objects_codec import format_indented, parse_indented\n# Format an object with an identifier\nformatted = format_indented(\n    '6dcf4c1b-ff3f-482c-95ab-711ea7d1b019',\n    {'uuid': '6dcf4c1b-ff3f-482c-95ab-711ea7d1b019', 'status': 'executed'}\n)\n# Parse it back\nid, obj = parse_indented(formatted)\n```\n**Rust:**\n```rust\nuse lino_objects_codec::format::{format_indented_ordered, parse_indented};\n// Format an object with an identifier\nlet pairs = [(\"status\", \"executed\"), (\"exitCode\", \"0\")];\nlet formatted = format_indented_ordered(\"my-uuid\", &pairs, \"  \").unwrap();\n// Parse it back\nlet (id, obj) = parse_indented(&formatted).unwrap();\n```\n**C#:**\n```csharp\nusing Lino.Objects.Codec;\n// Format an object with an identifier\nvar obj = new Dictionary<string, string?> { { \"status\", \"executed\" }, { \"exitCode\", \"0\" } };\nvar formatted = Format.FormatIndented(\"my-uuid\", obj);\n// Parse it back\nvar (id, parsedObj) = Format.ParseIndented(formatted);\n```\n## How It Works\nThe library uses the [links-notation](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation) format as the serialization target. Each object is encoded as a Link with type information:\n### Readable format (the default)\nIn every language `encode()` writes one `( )` construct for both objects and\narrays, at every level including the root. Lines of the form `key value` make an\nobject, bare-value lines make an array:\n```lino\n(\n  name \"Alice\"",

The React adapter adds source `T`, named `Var`, branches,\nplurals and locale-aware formatting. Source extraction, catalog validation and\ntranslation-provider candidates are available through the CLI and a Vite/Rollup\nplugin. Rust adds source/deferred messages and an optional ICU engine.\nSee the [source-message guide](docs/source-messages.md),\n[framework boundaries](docs/framework-integrations.md) and\n[GT capability study](docs/case-studies/issue-25/README.md) for examples and\nexplicit coverage limits. Existing keyed translation APIs remain available.\n## Why Links Notation?\nTranslation files are not data — they are content. JSON is brittle for that\njob: every value has to be wrapped in quotes, every nested key needs braces,\nand a missing comma breaks the whole file. `.lino` is a quoted-string + nested\nidentifier format that makes large catalogues comfortable to read in plain\ntext and trivial to diff.\n```lino\nen\n  greeting \"Hello, {{name}}!\"\n  telegram\n    help\n      title \"Help\"\n      solve\n        alias\n          detail \"Tool aliases imply `--tool <tool>`\"\n  prompt\n    system\n      general\n        guidelines\n          header \"General guidelines.\"\n          body \"\"\"\n            When you start, create a detailed plan for yourself.\n            Follow your todo list step by step.\n          \"\"\"\n  error\n    label \"Error\"\n    invalid\n      github\n        url \"Error: Invalid GitHub URL format\"\n  cart\n    title \"Your cart\"\n    items\n      zero \"Your cart is empty\"\n      one \"{{count}} item\"\n      other \"{{count}} items\"\n  role\n    male \"He is a developer\"\n    female \"She is a developer\"\n    other \"They are a developer\"\n```\nThe loader flattens that catalogue to runtime keys like\n`telegram.help.solve.alias.detail`,\n`prompt.system.general.guidelines.body`, `error.label`,\n`error.invalid.github.url`, `cart.items_one`, and `role_female`, so deeply\nnested authoring still resolves stable flat runtime keys.\nA nested group's `label` child is also exposed as the parent key, so\n`error.label` and `error` both resolve to `\"Error\"` while an explicit `error`\nentry still takes precedence. The Hive Mind migration that motivated this\npattern is summarized in\n[docs/case-studies/issue-12](./docs/case-studies/issue-12).\n### Migration aliases\nProjects that migrate older mixed dot/underscore keys to deeper `.lino`\nnesting can opt into generated compatibility aliases:\n```js\nconst catalogues = await loadLocalesFromDirectory('./locales', {\n  compatibilityAliases: ['collapseTail', 'parentLabel'],\n});\nconst i18n = createI18n({ locales: catalogues, defaultLocale: 'en' });\n```\nWith `collapseTail`, a canonical key such as\n`telegram.help.solve.alias.detail` also exposes\n`telegram.help_solve_alias_detail`, `telegram.help.solve_alias_detail`, and\n`telegram.help.solve.alias_detail`. With `parentLabel`, `error.label` also\nexposes `error`. Explicit catalogue entries always win over generated aliases.\nThe full design rationale lives in [docs/case-studies/issue-1](./docs/case-studies/issue-1).\n## Quick start\n### JavaScript\n```bash\ncd js\nnpm install\nnpm test\n```\n```js\nimport { createI18n } from 'lino-i18n';\nimport { loadLocalesFromDirectory } from 'lino-i18n/loaders';\nconst catalogues = await loadLocalesFromDirectory('./locales');\nconst i18n = createI18n({\n  locales: catalogues,\n  defaultLocale: 'en',\n  fallback: ['en'],\n});\ni18n.t('greeting', { name: 'World' });              // → \"Hello, World!\"\ni18n.t('cart.items', { count: 0 });                 // → \"Your cart is empty\"\ni18n.t('cart.items', { count: 3 }, { locale: 'ru' }); // → \"3 товара\"\n```\nFor nested catalogs such as `locales/prompts/system/`, pass\n`{ recursive: true }` to `loadLocalesFromDirectory`. This opt-in traversal merges\nby the locale declared in each file. See the [directory loading guide](js/README.md#nested-locale-directories)\nfor deterministic ordering, duplicate-key precedence and compatibility aliases.\n### Rust\n```bash\ncd rust\ncargo test\ncargo run --example basic",

It accepts\nisolated environment maps and a base directory, selectively maps typed options\nto environment variables, and supports allowlisted secret files. The\n`lino-arguments/pure` entry resolves plain objects in browser/WASM contexts\nwithout Node filesystem access. See the JavaScript documentation for precedence.\nUse `makeConfig({ includePositionals: true })` to also return yargs' positional\ncommand arguments in `config.positionals`.\nRust retains its clap/process-based configuration APIs; isolated contexts and\nsecret-file settings are currently JavaScript capabilities. This repository has\nno Python package.\n```bash\nnpm install lino-arguments\n```\n```javascript\nimport { makeConfig } from 'lino-arguments';\nconst config = makeConfig({\n  yargs: ({ yargs, getenv }) =>\n    yargs.option('port', { default: getenv('PORT', 3000) }),\n});\n```\nSee [js/README.md](js/) for full documentation.\n### Rust\nThe Rust version uses clap for argument parsing.\n```toml\n[dependencies]\nlino-arguments = \"0.2\"\n```\n```rust\nuse clap::Parser;\nuse lino_arguments::{getenv_int, getenv_bool};\n#[derive(Parser)]\nstruct Args {\n    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = getenv_int(\"PORT\", 3000) as u16)]\n    port: u16,\n}\n```\nSee [rust/README.md](rust/) for full documentation.\n## Repository Structure\n```\nlino-arguments/\n├── js/                    # JavaScript implementation\n│   ├── src/              # Source code\n│   ├── tests/            # Tests\n│   ├── examples/         # Usage examples\n│   ├── .changeset/       # Changesets for JS releases\n│   └── package.json      # npm package config\n├── rust/                  # Rust implementation\n│   ├── src/              # Source code\n│   ├── tests/            # Integration tests\n│   ├── changelog.d/      # Changelog fragments for Rust releases\n│   └── Cargo.toml        # Cargo package config\n├── scripts/              # Shared release/CI scripts\n├── .github/workflows/    # CI/CD workflows\n│   ├── js.yml           # JavaScript CI/CD\n│   └── rust.yml         # Rust CI/CD\n└── docs/                 # Documentation\n```\n## Development\n### JavaScript\n======== lino-env\n# lino-env\nA library to operate .lenv files - an alternative to .env files that uses `: ` (colon-space) instead of `=` for key-value separation.\n**Available in both JavaScript and Rust!**\n## What are .lenv files?\n.lenv files are configuration files similar to .env files, but with a different syntax:\n```\n# .env format (traditional)\nGITHUB_TOKEN=[REDACTED]\n# .lenv format (this library)\nGITHUB_TOKEN: [REDACTED]\n```\nThe key difference is the use of `: ` separator, which aligns with [links-notation](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation) format. If a key appears multiple times, the last value wins (rewrite semantics).\n## Packages\n| Package            | Language   | Directory | Status                                                                                  |\n| ------------------ | ---------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n## JavaScript Package\n### Installation\n```bash\nnpm install lino-env\n```\n### Quick Start\n```bash\n# create .lenv file\necho \"HELLO: World\" > .lenv\n# create index.js\necho \"import linoenv from 'lino-env'; linoenv.config(); console.log('Hello ' + process.env.HELLO)\" > index.js\n# run\nnode index.js\n```\nOutput:\n```\nHello World\n```\n### Usage\n```javascript\nimport linoenv from 'lino-env';\nlinoenv.config();\nconsole.log(`Hello ${process.env.HELLO}`);\n```\nFor full API documentation, see the [JavaScript README](./js/README.md) (coming soon) or the source code.\n## Rust Package\n### Installation\nAdd this to your `Cargo.toml`:\n```toml\n[dependencies]\nlino-env = \"0.1\"\n```\n### Quick Start\n```rust\nuse lino_env::LinoEnv;\n// Create and write a new .lenv file\nlet mut env = LinoEnv::new(\".lenv\");\nenv.set(\"GITHUB_TOKEN\", \"gh_abc123\");\nenv.set(\"API_KEY\", \"my_api_key\");\nenv.write().unwrap();\n// Read an existing .lenv file\nlet mut env = LinoEnv::new(\".lenv\");\nenv.read().unwrap();\n// Get a value\nif let Some(token) = env.get(\"GITHUB_TOKEN\") {\n    println!(\"Token: {}\", token);\n}\n```\nFor full API documentation, see the [Rust README](./rust/README.md).\n## File Format\n.lenv files use the following format:\n- Key-value separator: `: ` (colon followed by space)\n- One key-value pair per line\n======== lino-schema\n# js-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template\nA comprehensive template for AI-driven JavaScript/TypeScript development with full CI/CD pipeline support.\n## Features\n- **Multi-runtime support**: Works with Bun, Node.js, and Deno\n- **Universal testing**: Uses [test-anywhere](https://github.com/link-foundation/test-anywhere) for cross-runtime tests\n- **Automated releases**: Changesets-based versioning with GitHub Actions\n- **Code quality**: ESLint + Prettier with pre-commit hooks via Husky\n- **Package manager agnostic**: Works with bun, npm, yarn, pnpm, and deno\n- **Broken link checks**: Automated link validation with [lychee](https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action) and Web Archive fallback suggestions\n## Quick Start\n### Using This Template\n1. Install dependencies: `bun install`\n6. It aims to be as customizable as\n[GraphQL](https://graphql.org), yet simpler, more universal, and more adaptive —\nin the spirit of [link-cli](https://github.com/link-foundation/link-cli).\nWhere GraphQL needs separate query, mutation, and subscription type systems,\nLinksQL expresses **read, create, update, and delete** with one operation:\npairing a _restriction_ (what to match) with a _substitution_ (what it becomes).\n```\n(restriction) (substitution)\n```\nThat single rule is Turing-complete (it is a Markov algorithm over an\nassociative store), so it scales from one-line reads to complex multi-pattern\nrewrites without new syntax.\n## Data model: links and doublets\nEverything is a **link** — an ordered pair stored as `(index: source target)`,\nwhere `index`, `source`, and `target` are positive integers referring to other\nlinks. A link that points at itself, `(i: i i)`, is a **point** — the atom of\nthe model. This is the _doublet_ associative model used across\n[deep-foundation](https://github.com/deep-foundation) and\n[link-foundation](https://github.com/link-foundation).\nLinks are written and parsed with **Links Notation (LiNo)**:\n```\n(1: 1 1)            // a point with index 1\n(3: 1 2)            // link 3 connects 1 -> 2\n((alice loves) bob) // names auto-create as points; doublets nest for arity > 2\n($i: $s $t)         // $-prefixed tokens are variables for matching\n(*: * *)            // * is a wildcard that matches anything\n```\nBecause a link has exactly two endpoints, every pattern carries **0 or 2\nvalues** (an optional `index:` prefix aside). Higher-order relations are built by\nnesting: \"alice loves bob\" is `((alice loves) bob)` — the link `(alice loves)` is\n======== transformer\n# transformer\nA rule-based, Turing-complete structural transformer built on\n[Links Notation](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation) (LiNo).\nBoth the data and the rewrite rules are written in LiNo. The transformer applies\nordered pattern/replacement rules to link structures. Unlike its text-and-regex\npredecessor\n[`RegularExpressions.Transformer`](https://github.com/linksplatform/RegularExpressions.Transformer),\nmatching is **structural and identity-aware** rather than textual, so equivalent\nformatting yields identical matches.\n## Quick start\nBuild the crate and run one of the shipped example programs, feeding input on\nstandard input:\n```sh\necho \"(a before b)\" | cargo run -- run --program examples/swap.lino\n# => (b before a)\n```\nCompute `2 + 1` with unary (Peano) arithmetic:\n```sh\necho \"(add (s (s z)) (s z))\" | cargo run -- run --program examples/peano-add.lino\n# => (s (s (s z)))\n```\nSimulate a 2-state busy-beaver Turing machine — the universality demonstration —\nwhich halts after exactly six steps leaving four `1`s on the tape:\n```sh\necho \"(tm e A 0 e)\" | cargo run -- run --program examples/turing-bb2.lino --trace\n# => (tm (c 1 (c 1 e)) H 1 (c 1 e))\n```\nSee [`examples/README.md`](examples/README.md) for the full walkthrough.\n## Writing a program\nA program is a LiNo document of ordered rules. An LLM generates a JSON specification constrained to that catalog. A catalog can also be exported as JSON Schema for LLM structured-output APIs. One third-party guide says props are validated against Zod schemas at runtime.\n- **Origin and license:** The project launched in January 2026 under Apache 2.0. The project has already accumulated over 13,000 stars on GitHub since its January 2026 launch. A SourcePulse listing shows about 14,488 stars, so the counts vary by snapshot date.\n- **Platforms:** Renders for React, Vue, Svelte, React Native, PDF, email, and video from a unified catalog. Packages are published under the @json-render npm scope, and the shadcn preset offers a production-ready catalog of 36 components with Zod schemas already defined.\n- **Streaming:** A SpecStream compiler supports streaming AI responses and progressive UI rendering.\n- **Criticism:** Some developers questioned the design. Some developers questioned why Vercel would \"reinvent it as a new system\" when existing standards like OpenAPI and JSON Schema already describe data structures.\n- **Comparison with A2UI:** One Medium comparison describes json-render as a \"tool\" tightly coupled to a specific application's component set, while A2UI positions itself as a \"protocol\" for cross-agent interoperability.\n\nThe sources are mostly news articles, a SourcePulse summary, and community guides. The skill-registry pages (skills.cat, sharedcontext.ai) are third-party, not Vercel documentation. [2026-11-01T11:36:36.159Z] [INFO]           "content": "# Existing solutions: prior art, libraries and specifications\n\nResearch for [link-foundation/ui#1](https://github.com/link-foundation/ui/issues/1),\n\"Initial version of associative UI framework\". Collected 2026-11-01.\n\nThis document lists components, libraries and specifications that solve parts of\nthe problem in issue #1. The issue asks for:\n\n- one Links Notation (LiNo) dialect for structure, config, styles, animations;\n- animation recording;\n- a WYSIWYG designer and a development/configuration mode;\n- classic UIs as themes;\n- Material, Fluent and Apple HIG alignment;\n- our own controls, charts, diagrams and links-network visualisation;\n- vanilla JS, React, React Native, Vue, Swift and Kotlin targets;\n- public-domain assets of our own;\n- a self-hosted documentation site.\n\n## How to read the tables\n\nEach entry gives a one-line description, the license, a URL and a relevance tag.\nThe tags mean:\n\n| Tag | Meaning |\n|-----|---------|\n| **ADOPT** | Depend on it, or embed it, in shipped packages. The license is permissive (MIT, ISC, BSD, Apache-2.0, CC0) and the project is healthy. |\n| **INTEROP** | Import from it, export to it, or provide an adapter for it. Do not make it a core dependency. |\n| **LEARN** | Study its design, data model or user experience. Do not depend on it. |\n| **AVOID** | The license or terms conflict with our goals (public domain, no-code designer, cross-platform), or it is unmaintained. |\n\nFacts marked **(verify)** were not confirmed against a primary source, or the\nsources disagree. Re-check them before relying on them in an issue or in code.\n\nThe license for our own code and assets is assumed to be **Unlicense** (code)\nand **CC0-1.0** (assets). That matches the issue's \"fully public domain\"\nrequirement. Every dependency must be compatible with redistribution inside\npublic-domain packages, which means permissive licenses only. Copyleft\ndependencies (MPL, EPL, LGPL) are acceptable only as optional, separately\npackaged adapters.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Declarative and serialisable UI description formats\n\nThese are the closest prior art for \"any UI framework is just a Links Notation\ndocument\". Most use JSON with a **component catalog**: the document names\ncomponents from a trusted registry, and each platform renders them natively.\nA LiNo dialect can follow the same pattern.\n\n| Name | What it is | License | URL | Tag | Why |\n|------|-----------|---------|-----|-----|-----|\n| Adaptive Cards | Microsoft JSON schema for platform-agnostic UI cards (schema 1.6), with host config for theming and renderers for JS, .NET, iOS and Android | MIT (verify) | https://adaptivecards.io, https://github.com/microsoft/AdaptiveCards | LEARN + INTEROP | Proves that one JSON tree plus a separate \"host config\" (theme) can render natively everywhere. Its rule that renderers declare a supported schema version and fall back to `fallbackText` is a good versioning model for our dialect. Teams caps support at 1.5, so hosts drift. Provide an importer. |\n| Google A2UI (Agent-to-User Interface) | Agents send declarative JSON that names components from a trusted client catalog; the client renders native widgets. Transport-agnostic (A2A, AG-UI, SSE, WebSocket) | Apache-2.0 | https://a2ui.org, https://github.com/google/A2UI | LEARN + INTEROP | Closest match to \"explain UI to agents\". Uses data, not code, for safety, plus a component catalog and streaming incremental updates. v0.8 stable, v0.9 draft (verify the current version). Map A2UI messages to and from our LiNo dialect so agents that speak A2UI can drive our UI. |\n| Vercel json-render | Generative-UI framework. The LLM emits JSON constrained to a Zod-defined catalog. Renderers for React, Vue, Svelte, React Native, PDF and email. Launched January 2026 | Apache-2.0 | https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render | LEARN | Shows catalog-to-JSON-Schema export for LLM structured output, and streaming (\"SpecStream\"). Our catalog should also export a schema that agents can target. |\n| Airbnb Ghost Platform (GP) | Airbnb's internal server-driven UI: GraphQL-delivered sections, screens and actions rendered on web, iOS and Android | Proprietary (internal) | https://medium.com/airbnb-engineering/a-deep-dive-into-airbnbs-server-driven-ui-system-842244c5f5 | LEARN | Shows the value of \"sections + screens + actions\" as a shared vocabulary across platforms. Not available to use. |\n| DivKit (Yandex) | Server-driven UI framework. JSON layouts with variables, actions, animations and state, rendered natively on Android, iOS, Web and Flutter. Builders in TS, Kotlin and Python | Apache-2.0 | https://divkit.tech, https://github.com/divkit/divkit | LEARN (strong) | The most complete open SDUI. Native renderers on all of our target platforms, a declarative animation and transition model, variables and expressions, and a playground editor. A good benchmark for feature coverage of our dialect. |\n| Remote Flutter Widgets (rfw) | Official Flutter package for rendering widget trees described in a text or binary format at runtime | BSD-3-Clause | https://pub.dev/packages/rfw | LEARN | Has both a text format and a compact binary format for the same tree, similar to LiNo text versus a doublets store. Has a \"local widget library\" registry. |\n| Airbnb Lona | Earlier cross-platform component description format and compiler (JSON to Swift, Kotlin, React) | MIT, archived | https://github.com/airbnb/Lona | LEARN | A cautionary tale: a one-format-to-every-platform code generator that was abandoned. Prefer runtime interpretation plus thin native renderers over heavy code generation. |\n| JSON Forms (EclipseSource) | Forms generated from JSON Schema (data) plus a UI schema (layout), with renderer sets for React, Angular and Vue | MIT | https://jsonforms.io | LEARN + INTEROP | Separates data schema from UI schema and lets you swap renderer sets. Use the same split for our form controls. An importer is cheap to add. |\n| Lottie / Bodymovin | JSON vector-animation format exported from After Effects. Lottie spec v1.0 published September 2024 by the Lottie Animation Community (Linux Foundation / Joint Development Foundation) | Spec: open (LAC). lottie-web: MIT. lottie-ios and lottie-android: Apache-2.0 | https://lottie.github.io, https://github.com/airbnb/lottie-web | INTEROP (import/export) | A standard, serialisable, keyframed animation format. Our animation model should round-trip to Lottie for vector animations. Spec 1.0 excludes text layers, effects and expressions; 1.1 plans interactivity and accessibility. |\n| dotLottie / ThorVG | Zipped Lottie container with state machines. ThorVG is a lightweight vector renderer | MIT (verify per repo) | https://dotlottie.io, https://github.com/thorvg/thorvg | INTEROP | State-machine interactivity on top of Lottie. Useful as a reference for interactive animation states. |\n| Rive | Interactive vector animation with state machines. Proprietary binary `.riv` format and a hosted editor. Open runtimes for web, iOS, Android, Flutter and React Native | Runtimes MIT. Editor and export proprietary (paid plan for export, verify) | https://rive.app, https://github.com/rive-app | LEARN; AVOID as a core format | Its state-machine model (inputs, states, blend states, listeners) is the best design reference for interactive animation. The format and editor are closed, so do not build our animation format on it. |\n| XAML (WPF, WinUI, MAUI, Avalonia, Uno) | XML markup for object trees, with data binding, styles, templates, resources and visual states | WPF, MAUI and Avalonia: MIT. Uno: Apache-2.0 | https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/desktop/wpf/xaml/, https://avaloniaui.net | LEARN (strong) | The model behind the Visual Studio designer. Has attached properties, resource dictionaries, control templates (a theme replaces a control's whole visual tree), VisualStateManager, and design-time-only attributes (`d:`). Our dialect needs each of these concepts. |\n| QML (Qt Quick) | Declarative, JSON-like object language with property bindings, states, transitions and behaviours. Qt Design Studio round-trips it | LGPL-3.0 / GPL / commercial | https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qmlapplications.html | LEARN; AVOID as a dependency | Bindings, `states` and `transitions` are first-class in the language, and the designer edits the same file. That is the target architecture: designer and code share one source. The license is copyleft or commercial. |\n| SwiftUI | Apple declarative UI: views are values, with modifiers, environment, `@State`/`@Observable` and animations | Proprietary Apple framework (free to use on Apple platforms) | https://developer.apple.com/xcode/swiftui/ | INTEROP (Swift renderer target) | The native target for the Swift implementation. Map our tree to the modifier chain. Previews are the designer reference (section 3). |\n| Jetpack Compose | Kotlin declarative UI with composables, modifiers, CompositionLocals and an animation API | Apache-2.0 | https://developer.android.com/jetpack/compose | INTEROP (Kotlin renderer target) | The native target for the Kotlin implementation. Compose Multiplatform extends it to iOS, desktop and web (section 9). |\n| Mitosis (Builder.io) | Write a component once in a JSX subset and compile it to React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, Solid, Qwik, Swift (experimental) and others | MIT | https://mitosis.builder.io, https://github.com/BuilderIO/mitosis | LEARN; optional ADOPT for codegen | Shows a framework-neutral component IR (JSON) with per-framework generators. Most targets are still beta (verify). Repository activity slowed in 2025. Use it only to generate thin wrappers, and keep our own LiNo IR as the source of truth. |\n| Web Components (Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, templates) | Browser-native component model | W3C/WHATWG standards | https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Web_components | ADOPT | The natural target for \"vanilla JS\". One custom-element set can be wrapped for React 19 (native custom-element support), Vue and Angular. |\n| Lit | Small library for building Web Components with reactive properties and templates | BSD-3-Clause | https://lit.dev | ADOPT (candidate) | Small, fast, Google-maintained. Has SSR (`@lit-labs/ssr`) and context. A strong candidate base for the vanilla-JS renderer. |\n| Stencil | Web Component compiler that generates React, Vue and Angular output wrappers. Used by Ionic | MIT | https://stenciljs.com | LEARN / ADOPT (wrapper generation) | Its \"output targets\" pattern auto-generates framework wrappers from one Web Component set. Exactly the distribution model we need. |\n| Custom Elements Manifest | JSON description of a custom element's properties, events, slots, CSS parts and CSS properties | Open schema (verify license) | https://github.com/webcomponents/custom-elements-manifest | ADOPT (as an export) | Storybook and IDEs read it. Our component catalog (in LiNo) should be able to emit it. This is the metadata the designer's property grid needs. |\n| AG-UI / MCP Apps | Agent-UI event protocols. MCP Apps (2025) lets MCP servers return interactive UI | MIT / open specs (verify) | https://docs.ag-ui.com, https://modelcontextprotocol.io | INTEROP (later) | Transport targets for agent-driven UI once the A2UI mapping exists. |\n\n**Takeaways for the dialect.** Every successful format here separates five\nthings:\n\n1. a structure tree (component plus props plus children);\n2. a component catalog or schema;\n3. a theme or host config (tokens);\n4. state and bindings;\n5. actions and events.\n\nThe ones with designers (XAML, QML) add design-time-only metadata and visual\nstates. Our LiNo dialect should name these five layers explicitly. It should be\nlossless to and from JSON, so A2UI, Adaptive Cards and JSON Forms import is\nmechanical.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Design tokens and design-system guidelines\n\n| Name | What it is | License | URL | Tag | Why |\n|------|-----------|---------|-----|-----|-----|\n| W3C Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG) Format Module **2025.10** | First **stable** design-token interchange format, published 2025-10-28. JSON with `$value`, `$type`, `$description`, aliases (`{group.token}`) and composite types. Has companion Color and Resolver modules (themes and modes). It is a Community Group report, not a W3C Recommendation | W3C Community Final Spec Agreement | https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/, https://www.w3.org/community/design-tokens/2025/10/28/design-tokens-specification-reaches-first-stable-version/ | ADOPT (as the interchange format) | Figma, Penpot, Tokens Studio, Style Dictionary and Terrazzo support it. Our LiNo token dialect must round-trip losslessly to DTCG JSON. The Resolver Module gives a standard way to express light/dark, density and brand themes, which is our \"classic UI as themes\" requirement. |\n| Style Dictionary (v4/v5) | Token build system that transforms tokens to CSS, JS, Swift, Kotlin/Compose, Android XML and more. DTCG-aware | Apache-2.0 | https://styledictionary.com, https://github.com/amzn/style-dictionary | ADOPT | Already generates platform outputs for every one of our targets. Write a LiNo parser or preprocessor and reuse its transforms and formats. |\n| Terrazzo (formerly Cobalt UI) | DTCG-native token compiler (CSS, Sass, JS, Swift, plugins) | MIT (verify) | https://terrazzo.app | LEARN / alternative | A stricter DTCG implementation. Use it to cross-check our DTCG output. |\n| Tokens Studio | Figma plugin and platform for managing DTCG tokens, with GitHub sync. Co-built Penpot's native tokens | Plugin open source (verify license). Platform commercial | https://tokens.studio | INTEROP | Designers already use it. DTCG compatibility gives interop for free. |\n| Material Design 3 (incl. M3 Expressive, 2025) | Google design system: color roles, dynamic color (HCT), type scale, shape, motion, elevation, state layers; tokens published as `md.sys.*` / `md.ref.*` | Guidelines: Google docs (content generally CC BY 4.0, verify). `material-color-utilities`: Apache-2.0 | https://m3.material.io, https://github.com/material-foundation/material-color-utilities | ADOPT (tokens + color utils) / LEARN (guidelines) | MUI migration path. Ship a \"material\" theme that maps `md.sys.*` roles onto our semantic tokens. Use material-color-utilities to generate palettes from a seed color. |\n| Material UI (MUI) | The most-used React implementation of Material. Theme object, `sx` prop, slots | MIT (core). MUI X Pro/Premium commercial | https://mui.com | INTEROP (migration source) | The issue explicitly asks for easy migration from MUI. Write a converter from an MUI theme to LiNo tokens and a component-name mapping table. Avoid MUI X commercial tiers. |\n| Fluent 2 (Microsoft) | Microsoft design system. Tokens in global and alias layers (`colorNeutralBackground1` and so on), Fluent UI React v9, Fluent UI Web Components, iOS and Android libraries | MIT (fluentui repos) | https://fluent2.microsoft.design, https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui | ADOPT (tokens) / LEARN | A well-structured alias-token naming scheme that suits our semantic layer. Ship a \"fluent\" theme. Its high-contrast theme is a good accessibility reference. |\n| Apple Human Interface Guidelines | Apple platform guidelines: layout, typography (SF), materials, motion, accessibility, platform idioms | Proprietary documentation. SF fonts and SF Symbols have restricted licenses | https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines | LEARN only | Follow the guidance (spacing, hit targets, semantic colors, Dynamic Type) in an \"apple\" theme. On Apple platforms, use system fonts and symbols at runtime. Never bundle SF Pro or SF Symbols in our cross-platform packages (section 8). |\n| Open UI (W3C Community Group) | Researches common component anatomy and names across design systems; drives new HTML controls (customizable `<select>`, popover, invoker commands) | W3C CG | https://open-ui.org | LEARN (strong) | Its \"component research\" pages compare the same component across about 20 design systems. Use it to choose canonical component and part names for our catalog. That naming is what makes Material, Fluent and HIG themes interchangeable. |\n\n**Takeaway.** Use a three-layer token model. LiNo is the source, and DTCG\n2025.10 is the exchange format.\n\n1. Reference: raw palette and scales.\n2. Semantic (system): roles such as `surface`, `on-surface` and `primary`.\n3. Component: for example `button.primary.background`.\n\nMaterial, Fluent, HIG and \"classic\" themes (Windows 95, Aqua and so on) are then\njust alternative reference and semantic layers, plus optional\ncontrol-template overrides (the XAML idea).\n\n---\n\n## 3. WYSIWYG and visual builders, designers and dev-mode inspectors\n\n| Name | What it is | License | URL | Tag | Why |\n|------|-----------|---------|-----|-----|-----|\n| GrapesJS | Framework-agnostic web page builder: block manager, style manager, layer manager, trait (property) manager, device preview; stores the project as JSON | BSD-3-Clause | https://grapesjs.com, https://github.com/GrapesJS/grapesjs | LEARN (strong); possible ADOPT for an early prototype | Its four panels (blocks, styles, layers, traits) are the standard information architecture for a web designer. Its JSON component model maps well to LiNo. It is DOM-oriented and opinionated, so long term our designer should be native to our own model. |\n| Puck | Modular visual editor for React. Data is a JSON tree of your own components; config declares fields per component | MIT | https://puckeditor.com, https://github.com/puckeditor/puck | LEARN (strong) / ADOPT for the React prototype | Uses a component config, a JSON tree and your own components, the same split as our catalog plus LiNo tree. Small and permissive, so a fast way to get a React designer before our own exists. |\n| Craft.js | React framework for building page editors: drag-and-drop, serialisable node tree, per-component \"related\" settings panels | MIT | https://craft.js.org, https://github.com/prevwong/craft.js | LEARN | Clean serialised node-graph model with resolver mapping (name to component), the same as our catalog lookup. Releases are less frequent (verify activity). |\n| Plasmic | Visual builder for React with code components, variants, slots and codegen or a headless loader | Mixed: most code MIT, `platform/` AGPL (verify) | https://plasmic.app, https://github.com/plasmicapp/plasmic | LEARN; AVOID the AGPL parts | Strong \"variants\" model (hover, pressed, custom variants) and \"register your own code component\" flow. Do not copy AGPL platform code. |\n| Builder.io (Visual Editor, SDKs) | Hosted visual CMS and editor, with open SDKs for many frameworks; \"Visual Copilot\" Figma-to-code | SDKs MIT. Editor proprietary SaaS | https://www.builder.io | LEARN; AVOID as a dependency | Its \"register components, then edit visually on your live site\" model is close to our dev mode, but the editor is closed and hosted. |\n| Webflow | Hosted no-code site designer with CSS-class-based styling and interactions; owns GSAP since 2024 | Proprietary SaaS | https://webflow.com | LEARN (UX only) | Best-in-class box-model, flex and grid style panels and class-combo UX. Note its GSAP license restriction (section 6). |\n| Figma Dev Mode | Inspect mode for developers: measurements, tokens/variables, code snippets, Code Connect (links design components to code components) | Proprietary SaaS | https://www.figma.com/dev-mode/ | LEARN + INTEROP | Code Connect is the pattern for mapping design components to our catalog. Figma Variables export to DTCG gives token interop. |\n| Penpot | Open-source design and prototyping tool. SVG/CSS-native, native design tokens (DTCG) since 2.6, plugin API, self-hostable | MPL-2.0 | https://penpot.app, https://github.com/penpot/penpot | INTEROP (primary design tool); LEARN | An open alternative to Figma. Its tokens use DTCG via Tokens Studio. Recommend it as the designer-facing tool, with a LiNo/DTCG token sync. MPL is file-level copyleft, so integrate through its API and file formats rather than copying code. |\n| tldraw SDK | Infinite-canvas whiteboard SDK: shapes, bindings, tools, multiplayer | Custom tldraw license. A **license key is required for production** since SDK 4.0 (September 2025). Commercial or hobby (watermark) licenses | https://tldraw.dev | LEARN; **AVOID as a dependency** | An excellent canvas architecture (shape utils, a store of records, bindings between shapes, much like links). Its license conflicts with public-domain redistribution. |\n| Excalidraw | Hand-drawn style whiteboard; embeddable React component; JSON scene format | MIT | https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw | ADOPT (diagram/whiteboard embed) / LEARN | A permissive canvas with a simple JSON element model. Suitable for a \"sketch\" diagram theme and as a reference for our own links canvas. |\n| Storybook (v10, October 2025, ESM-only) | Component workshop: stories, controls (an auto property grid from argTypes), docs, visual and accessibility tests, addons | MIT | https://storybook.js.org | ADOPT (for library development) / LEARN | Its controls panel is a property grid generated from component metadata, which is what our dev mode needs. Use Storybook for developing the React and Vue packages until our own docs site can host component playgrounds. Supports Web Components, React, Vue and React Native. |\n| React DevTools / Vue DevTools | Component-tree inspector, props and state editing, highlight on hover, \"jump to source\" | MIT | https://react.dev/learn/react-developer-tools, https://devtools.vuejs.org | LEARN (strong) | Our dev mode is \"DevTools for the LiNo tree\": select an element, edit its props or tokens live, then save a diff. Copy the select-element overlay and hover highlight UX. |\n| click-to-component / LocatorJS | Alt-click any element in a running app to open its source in the IDE | MIT (verify each) | https://github.com/ericclemmons/click-to-component, https://www.locatorjs.com | LEARN | The minimal form of \"enter configuration mode on any running site\". Each rendered node needs a stable ID that links back to its LiNo source. |\n| Onlook | Open-source \"Cursor for designers\": [REDACTED] editing of a running React/Next.js app that writes back to code | Apache-2.0 (verify) | https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook | LEARN | The closest open-source analogue to \"modify UI on the fly on any of our websites, then make it the default\". It edits code. We edit LiNo config, which is simpler and safer. |\n| Visual Studio designers (WinForms, WPF/XAML Designer, XAML Hot Reload, Live Visual Tree) | Drag-and-drop designers with a toolbox, property grid, document outline, snaplines, and live visual-tree editing of running apps | Proprietary IDE. WinForms and WPF runtimes MIT | https://learn.microsoft.com/visualstudio/xaml-tools/ | LEARN (the UX target named in the issue) | The issue names this as the reference. Key pieces: Toolbox, Properties grid (categorised, with type-specific editors), Document Outline, snaplines and alignment, Live Visual Tree / Live Property Explorer on a running app, and design-time data. |\n| Xcode Previews (`#Preview`) | Live, interactive previews of SwiftUI views in the editor, with variants (dark mode, Dynamic Type, devices) | Proprietary | https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/previews-in-xcode | LEARN | The variant matrix (theme × size × locale × accessibility) in the preview canvas should be a built-in docs and designer feature. |\n| Android Studio Layout Editor / Compose Preview | XML layout designer (Blueprint, constraint handles, attributes panel) and `@Preview` for Compose, including Live Edit | Android Studio: Apache-2.0 base, with Google terms for the SDK (verify) | https://developer.android.com/studio/write/layout-editor | LEARN | ConstraintLayout handles and the \"Blueprint\" mode are a good reference for editing layout constraints visually. |\n| Qt Design Studio | QML visual designer with timeline animation, states, and two-way sync with code | Commercial / GPL (verify) | https://www.qt.io/product/ui-design-tools | LEARN | A designer and animation timeline over a single declarative source. Our target, minus the license. |\n| Appsmith / ToolJet / Retool | Internal-tool builders: widget palette, property panes, bindings to data | Appsmith Apache-2.0; ToolJet AGPL-3.0; Retool proprietary (verify) | https://www.appsmith.com | LEARN | Data-binding UX (\"{{ query.data }}\" in any property) for app-style configuration. |\n\n**Takeaway.** Build our own designer over the LiNo tree. Reuse the standard\npanel architecture: Toolbox/Blocks, Layers/Outline, Properties/Traits,\nStyles/Tokens, a Timeline for animations, and Variants/States. Puck or GrapesJS\ncan speed up an early React prototype, but they must not become the source of\ntruth. Dev mode is a runtime overlay, like React DevTools combined with\nVisual Studio's Live Visual Tree. It requires every rendered node to carry a\nstable link ID that maps back to its LiNo source.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Expo SDK 54+ for apps and demos. |\n| Expo | RN toolchain and SDK, with web support via React Native Web | MIT | https://expo.dev | ADOPT (RN demo apps) | Easiest way to ship RN demos, including on the docs site. |\n| Lynx (ByteDance) | Cross-platform native UI framework (web-like CSS, dual-thread) | Apache-2.0 (verify) | https://lynxjs.org | LEARN | Shows web-like markup and styling rendered natively, close to \"DOM-like language rendered everywhere\". |\n| Flutter | Google's cross-platform UI toolkit (Material and Cupertino widgets, Impeller renderer) | BSD-3-Clause | https://flutter.dev | LEARN | Its Material and Cupertino widget sets show \"one tree, two platform looks\". Not a target in the issue. |\n| Capacitor | Native runtime that wraps web apps for iOS and Android with a plugin API | MIT | https://capacitorjs.com | INTEROP | Lets the vanilla-JS/Web Components implementation ship as a mobile app with no native renderer work. A reference for control templates. |\n\n**Takeaway.** Build the **reference implementation on the web**: Web Components\nplus a pure-JS LiNo runtime, with React and Vue wrappers generated in the\nStencil style. Add **React Native** (New Architecture) and **native SwiftUI and\nCompose renderers** that interpret the same LiNo documents and tokens. Compose\nMultiplatform can reduce iOS work, but keep SwiftUI native for HIG fidelity.\nCapacitor and Tauri are cheap shells for mobile and desktop demos, and Tauri\nfits the Rust associative stack.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Documentation and demo-site tooling (self-hosted on GitHub Pages)\n\n| Name | What it is | License | URL | Tag | Why |\n|------|-----------|---------|-----|-----|-----|\n| Vite | Dev server and bundler | MIT | https://vite.dev | ADOPT | Default build tool for the docs site and packages.
